Page 24 of 54 DE-EE0009512 Massachusetts Institute of Technology Project 4: Simplified and Stable Electron Transport Layer Based on Chemical Bath Deposition of SnO 2 Dense and conformal SnO electron transport layers (ETLs) deposited by chemical bath 2 deposition (CBD) have led to several record efficiency perovskite solar cells (PSC). CBD-grown layers, however, may contain ligand contaminants from the growth reaction, or unwanted impurities from the growth solution, and these may reduce device stability. As a result, the most stable n-i-p device structures are based on commercial SnO colloidal nanoparticles. Improving 2 the long-term stability of CBD grown tin oxide-based PSCs requires understanding the function of each component in the chemical bath reaction and the potential role of these components in device degradation processes. To date, all high efficiency CBD based tin oxide devices contain the following four components: SnCl -2H O, HCl, urea, and thioglycolic acid (TGA), a composition which can be 2 2 traced back to the fabrication of tin oxide electrodes for lithium-ion battery. Fluorine doped tin oxide (FTO) is preferred as the substrate because it is chemically compatible with the bath solution and functions as a natural seed layer to ensure a conformal and adherent deposition. Previous studies show the growth of the film is dominated by the attachment of nanocrystalline particles formed in the solution to the substrate. Thus, the essential part of this reaction is to control the kinetics of the tin oxide growth so that heterogeneous attachment of particles onto the substrate is favored over homogeneous precipitation in the solution. To deposit tin oxide selectively on the substrate, the initial pH of the bath solution is kept low enough by optimizing HCl concentration so that the hydrolysis of the metal ions is retarded. A slow and controlled hydrolysis is induced by the decomposition of urea at an elevated temperature. The reaction is stopped when bulk precipitation is observed; that is when particle sizes are too large to be incorporated into the film. During the deposition window, conditions for heterogeneous growth need to be optimized so that a film of desired thickness can be grown during the process. An essential consideration is that the attachment of particles formed in solution is affected by colloidal forces including van der Waals and electrostatic forces.
